questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: While a rising current initiates an impulse most effectively at the cathode, a FALL in current (when it occurs) is more effective at initiating an impulse at which electrode?

options.A: The cathode
options.B: The anode
options.C: Neither electrode is affected by a falling current
options.D: Both electrodes equally

questions.explanation: A fall in current is less effective overall at initiating an impulse than a rise, but when it does have an effect, it is the anode side of the nerve that is affected — so the anode produces greater stimulation than the cathode specifically in response to a falling current, the reverse of the pattern seen with a rising current.
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Electro Therapy

questions.question: A drug that reacts with an enzyme's catalytic site so strongly (via a covalent bond or very high affinity) that the normal substrate cannot displace it produces which kinetic pattern?

options.A: kM unchanged, Vmax unchanged (no real inhibition)
options.B: kM decreased, Vmax increased
options.C: kM increased and Vmax reduced — a non-equilibrium type of competitive inhibition
options.D: Only Vmax changes while kM decreases proportionally

questions.explanation: Classical competitive inhibition (equilibrium type) raises kM but leaves Vmax unchanged, since enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor. But when the inhibitor binds essentially irreversibly at the same catalytic site (e.g. organophosphates on cholinesterase, or methotrexate's very high affinity for dihydrofolate reductase), substrate can no longer displace it — this non-equilibrium type raises kM AND reduces Vmax.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology
questions.subject: Pharmacology

questions.question: Although prolactin levels are high throughout pregnancy, actual milk secretion does not begin until around the 3rd-4th postpartum day. What explains this delay?

options.A: Prolactin has no role in milk secretion at all
options.B: High circulating estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy make breast tissue unresponsive to prolactin; their withdrawal after delivery allows prolactin to act
options.C: The breasts are not anatomically ready until several days after birth
options.D: Oxytocin blocks prolactin receptors until labour is complete

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, the high circulating levels of estrogen and progesterone keep the fully-developed mammary glands unresponsive to prolactin, holding milk secretion in abeyance despite high prolactin levels. Once these steroids fall sharply after delivery, prolactin is free to begin its secretory (lactogenic) action.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Physiology of Lactation, Lactogenesis
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Why is the metaphysis of a growing long bone especially important clinically when it lies partly within a joint capsule?

options.A: It has no blood supply, so infection cannot spread there at all
options.B: Being an actively growing, richly vascularised part of the bone, infection there can spread into the joint if the metaphysis is intracapsular (and vice versa)
options.C: It is always extracapsular in every long bone, so it never affects joints
options.D: It only matters in the lower limb, not the upper limb

questions.explanation: The metaphysis is the actively growing part of the bone adjacent to the epiphyseal line, with a rich blood supply — making it a common site for infection in young people. Where the metaphysis is partly or wholly intracapsular (as at the upper end of the humerus), joint infection can spread to the metaphysis, and metaphyseal disease can spread into the joint.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Capsular Attachments and Epiphyseal Lines
questions.subject: Anatomy

questions.question: The Y-BOCS, a widely used clinical scale for OCD, stands for and is used to:

options.A: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale — elicit symptoms and rate severity of OCD
options.B: Young-Beck Obsessive Cognition Scale — diagnose depression only
options.C: Yale Behavioural Outcome Classification System — used only in research, never clinically
options.D: A scale exclusively for measuring anxiety, unrelated to OCD

questions.explanation: Y-BOCS stands for the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale, one of the most useful clinical tools for eliciting the range of obsessive and compulsive symptoms present and rating the overall severity of OCD.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — Clinical Syndromes
questions.subject: Psychiatry

questions.question: Lacunar strokes, caused by small penetrating-vessel disease deep in the cerebral white matter, are most strongly associated with which underlying conditions?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation and endocarditis only
options.B: Hypertensive small-vessel disease and diabetic microvascular disease
options.C: Congenital arteriovenous malformation
options.D: Berry aneurysm rupture

questions.explanation: Lacunar strokes result from small vessel (penetrating artery) disease deep in the cerebral white matter, and are strongly associated with chronic hypertension and diabetic microvascular disease, producing distinctive syndromes such as pure motor hemiplegia.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Lacunar Strokes
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: Exclusive breastfeeding provides approximately what level of contraceptive protection for the first 6 months postpartum?

options.A: About 20%
options.B: About 50%
options.C: About 98%
options.D: 0% — breastfeeding provides no contraceptive effect

questions.explanation: In a woman who is exclusively breastfeeding, lactational amenorrhoea provides approximately 98% contraceptive protection for up to 6 months postpartum — a recognised natural method of contraception, though ovulation can occasionally precede the return of menstruation.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Menstruation and Ovulation
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: The Nernst equation is used in physiology to calculate:

options.A: The equilibrium potential for a specific ion, based on its concentration gradient across the membrane
options.B: The total resting metabolic rate of a cell
options.C: The rate of action potential propagation along an axon
options.D: The molecular weight of an ion

questions.explanation: The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a given ion — the membrane potential at which the electrical force on that ion exactly balances its concentration gradient, so there is no net movement of that ion across the membrane.
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — The Equilibrium Potential
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: Which of the following is cited as a genuine limitation of mortality data, particularly relevant to developing countries like India?

options.A: Incomplete reporting of deaths and lack of accuracy in recording age/cause of death
options.B: Mortality data is always 100% complete and accurate worldwide
options.C: Death certificates do not exist in any country
options.D: Mortality data cannot be tabulated by any coding system

questions.explanation: Incomplete reporting of deaths is not usually a problem in developed countries, but can be considerable in India and other developing countries. Combined with inaccuracies in age/cause recording (often due to lack of diagnostic evidence, inexperienced certifying doctors, or absence of postmortem examination), this is a genuine limitation of mortality data quality.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — Limitations of Mortality Data
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: Persistence of red-coloured lochia well beyond the normal expected duration most likely signifies:

options.A: Normal healing with no clinical concern
options.B: Subinvolution of the uterus or retained bits of the conceptus
options.C: A completely normal variant seen in all women
options.D: Onset of the first postpartum menstrual period

questions.explanation: Persistence of the red colour of lochia beyond the normal limit is a clinically important sign suggesting subinvolution of the uterus or retained products of conception, and should prompt further evaluation.
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Lochia, Clinical Importance
questions.subject: OBGY

questions.question: Morning headaches in a patient with severe respiratory failure may signify:

options.A: Nocturnal carbon dioxide retention
options.B: Simple dehydration only
options.C: Normal sleep patterns with no pathology
options.D: Acute pulmonary embolism specifically

questions.explanation: Morning headaches in patients with severe respiratory failure may signify nocturnal carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia during sleep), which can be confirmed with early morning arterial blood gases or nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 monitoring.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Other Symptoms
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in General Medical & Surgical Condition

questions.question: Why can a meniscal injury sometimes present with little or no pain or swelling, making diagnosis more difficult?

options.A: The menisci are avascular and have no nerve supply on their inner two-thirds
options.B: The menisci are the most richly innervated structures in the knee
options.C: Meniscal tears always occur alongside complete ACL rupture, masking symptoms
options.D: Meniscal tissue regenerates immediately after injury

questions.explanation: The menisci are avascular and lack nerve supply on their inner two-thirds, meaning an injury confined to this region can produce little or no pain or swelling — one reason meniscal injury can be difficult to diagnose confidently without a thorough history and examination.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Meniscus Injury
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: When testing hip abductor strength in a patient with an unstable knee, resistance is applied at the distal femur (just above the knee) instead of at the ankle. Using this shorter lever, what is the highest grade that can be assigned, even if the patient tolerates maximal resistance?

options.A: Grade 5
options.B: Grade 4
options.C: Grade 3
options.D: Grade 2

questions.explanation: A shorter lever (resistance near the knee rather than at the ankle) makes the test mechanically easier, so a patient who takes maximal resistance in this position can still only be graded a 4 — the longer lever at the ankle is needed to truly demonstrate Grade 5 strength, since it better reflects the functional demand of gait.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing
questions.subject: Physical Diagnosis & Manipulative Skills

questions.question: Association areas of the cerebral cortex (in the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes) are now understood to primarily:

options.A: Simply form a direct wired connection between sensory input and motor output with no further processing
options.B: Process and integrate sensory information relayed from primary sensory areas and the thalamus, supporting complex functions like thought, memory, and language
options.C: Have no known function at all
options.D: Exist only in non-human animals, not in humans

questions.explanation: Early researchers thought association areas simply linked sensory input to motor output directly, but they are now understood to process and integrate information from primary sensory areas and the thalamus, supporting higher psychological functions such as thought, memory, imagery, and language before that processed information may be passed on to motor areas.
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Association Cortex, Behavior, and Experience
questions.subject: Psychology

questions.question: In the 'ischemic penumbra' surrounding the core of an acute ischemic stroke, neurons:

options.A: Die immediately within seconds, identical to the ischemic core
options.B: Survive for a somewhat longer period than core neurons, but will die without timely reperfusion — making this tissue a key target for acute treatment
options.C: Are completely unaffected by the stroke
options.D: Regenerate spontaneously without any intervention

questions.explanation: While neurons in the ischemic core die within minutes, the surrounding penumbra contains neurons that survive somewhat longer but remain at risk — cell survival depends on the severity and duration of ischemia, and without timely reperfusion, cells in the penumbra will die and the infarct will expand. This makes the penumbra the key target of emergency stroke treatment.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Pathophysiology
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Neurosciences

questions.question: On the International Death Certificate, Part II records:

options.A: The direct/immediate cause of death only
options.B: Other significant conditions that contributed to the death but were not directly related to the disease or condition causing it
options.C: The patient's full medical history
options.D: Only conditions unrelated to the patient's death in any way

questions.explanation: Part II of the death certificate records other significant associated conditions that contributed to the death but did not directly lead to it (e.g. diabetes as a contributing but non-causal condition), distinct from Part I, which records the direct cause and the underlying/antecedent causes forming the direct chain to death.
questions.sourceBook: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Measurement of Mortality — International Death Certificate
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Community Health

questions.question: The Gibbs-Donnan membrane equilibrium describes what happens when a membrane permeable to some ions separates two solutions, one of which also contains a non-diffusible (non-penetrating) ion such as a protein anion. What is the key consequence?

options.A: All ions distribute exactly equally on both sides regardless of the non-diffusible ion
options.B: The diffusible ions distribute asymmetrically at equilibrium — the diffusible cation concentration is higher on the side containing the non-penetrating anion
options.C: The non-diffusible ion eventually crosses the membrane too, given enough time
options.D: No electrical potential difference develops across the membrane

questions.explanation: When a non-diffusible anion (like a protein) is confined to one side, the freely diffusible ions (like K+ and Cl-) redistribute asymmetrically at equilibrium to maintain electrical neutrality and equal ion products on both sides — the diffusible cation ends up more concentrated on the side with the trapped anion. This asymmetry is the Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium and contributes to the resting membrane potential.
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Gibbs-Donnan Membrane Equilibrium
questions.subject: Physiology

questions.question: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) is used to assess for which type of knee instability?

options.A: Anterolateral rotary instability
options.B: Posterolateral rotary instability
options.C: Isolated medial collateral ligament sprain only
options.D: Patellofemoral instability

questions.explanation: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) tests for posterolateral rotary instability — a positive test (jerk in the knee, or posterior tibial shift with a 'giving way' sensation) indicates injury to the lateral collateral ligament, arcuate-popliteus complex, and mid-third of the lateral capsule.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Posterolateral Rotary Instability
questions.subject: Physiotherapy in Musculoskeletal Condition

questions.question: In a patient with a spinal cord injury who lacks active control of the back extensors, why might a therapist deliberately allow mild hypomobility to develop in the low back extensors while still fully stretching the hamstrings?

options.A: To create a stable, slightly shortened structure the patient can lean into for trunk support during long-term sitting
options.B: Because the back extensors cannot physically be stretched
options.C: To prevent contractures developing in the hamstrings only
options.D: Because stretching the trunk has no clinical value in this population

questions.explanation: This illustrates 'selective stretching': deliberately allowing some hypomobility in muscles the patient cannot actively control (like the back extensors after a thoracic/cervical spinal cord injury) gives them a stable structure to lean into for trunk stability while sitting, while the hamstrings are kept flexible enough for dressing and transfers.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Selective Stretching
questions.subject: Fundamentals of Exercise Therapy

questions.question: In the psychodynamic theory of OCD, the defense mechanism of 'undoing' is specifically responsible for the formation of:

options.A: Obsessions
options.B: Compulsions, which prevent or undo the feared consequences of the obsession
options.C: Phobic symptoms
options.D: Obsessive-compulsive personality traits only, never actual symptoms

questions.explanation: According to the psychodynamic theory, 'isolation of affect' contributes to the formation of obsessions themselves, while 'undoing' is the defense mechanism that produces compulsions — behaviours aimed at preventing or undoing the feared consequences the obsession represents. Displacement, by contrast, is linked to phobic symptom formation.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — Aetiology, Psychodynamic Theory
questions.subject: Psychiatry
